card.hook: Picture a ship the size of a building sitting calmly in a long stone-edged chamber, slowly rising while you watch. That's Gatun Locks, and the action is close enough that you don't need to squint.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Gatún Locks View Deck, the raised platform beside the locks, reached from the Agua Clara Visitor Center. Face along the chambers so the ship, the lock walls and Gatún Lake all fit in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to grab the chambers and the lake in one go. Switch to 1x for the ship in the chamber, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the bow or the lock gates.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, keep the lock walls level with them, and put the ship in the lower third with lake and sky above.
card.best_time: Go when a ship is due, because an empty chamber makes a pretty dull picture. Ask at the visitor centre when ships are expected that day.
card.selfie_here: If it's open, try the upper viewing platform of the Gatún Locks Visitors Pavilion, a high perch where the working locks sit behind you. The pedestrian lane on the Gatún Locks swing bridge is another option, since it's at the water line with the gates and ships behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the locks over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The viewing area has a lot of stairs, so it's not ideal if you have knee, ankle or back problems. Which viewing spot is open can change, so check on arrival, and check the official site for entry details.
card.challenge: Ships move slowly, so take three shots: a wide one, a close one, and a short Live Photo of the water level changing. Which one wins?
card.good_to_know: Gatun Locks is a working set of canal locks where ships are raised and lowered in three chambers, with Gatún Lake stretching away beyond. Entry to the View Deck is part of the Agua Clara ticket. Check the official site before you go for current details and opening times.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Gatún Locks View Deck, the raised platform beside the locks, reached from the Agua Clara Visitor Center. Face along the chambers so the ship, the lock walls and Gatún Lake all fit in one frame.

selfie_research.safety: One reviewer warns that the viewing area has a lot of stairs and is not suitable for people with knee, ankle or back problems.
selfie_research.notes: No page names a specific spot for a passer-by to photograph the visitor with the whole lock complex in view, so ask_someone_spot is null. The selfie spots are inferred from viewpoints the sources describe, not from a page that says 'shoot from here'. Sources conflict on status: Frommers lists the Visitors Pavilion as open daily 9am-4pm with free admission, while Madaboutpanama says the old visitor centre building is now closed. Canalmuseum says entry tickets are bought at the old Gatún visitor centre before going to the new Expansion Observation Center, and Visit Canal de Panamá lists the new Gatún Locks View Deck as part of the Agua Clara circuit at Calle Golf, which is a separate site. Pages found no rules on selfie sticks or tripods. One review says the writer strayed into a restricted area and was removed by security, but that is an anecdote, not a stated rule.

card.hook: Two tall towers, fans of cables and a long smooth deck, all stretched over a canal where real ships are working. The Atlantic Bridge looks a bit like a giant harp, and your phone will love it.
card.stand_here: Head for the Atlantic Bridge, where the phone icon marks the middle of the bridge outline, but only stop where it's legal and safe, because no pull-off is confirmed right there. Face back along the deck toward the Agua Clara side, then turn round for the Fort San Lorenzo side.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to squeeze a tower and the sweep of cables into one frame. Switch to 1x for the deck and towers, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the cable lines or the locks below.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the cables up with them so the towers stand straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Sunrise and sunset are a nice time for the bridge as a photo backdrop. Take a few frames of each view so you can pick the sharpest.
card.selfie_here: One page names a clear roadside space on the left after you cross the bridge, heading toward Fort San Lorenzo: turn left straight away and drive a few kilometres until you see a clear space to park on your left. Try the front camera at 0.5x with the bridge over your shoulder, but we haven't confirmed the bridge fits behind you there, and the views are mostly praised for the canal locks.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge carries heavy road traffic and there's little room to stop, so never stand on the carriageway and keep your phone away from the traffic side. If you visit the Agua Clara visitor centre for a calmer view of the whole bridge, check its official site first, as it may have its own entry rules.
card.challenge: Get both towers standing perfectly straight on your gridlines, then turn round and get the locks into a shot too. Bonus points if a ship sneaks in.
card.good_to_know: The Atlantic Bridge (Puente Atlántico) opened in 2019 and is the third bridge over the Panama Canal, after the Bridge of the Americas and the Centennial Bridge on the Pacific side. It's a cable-stayed bridge with two towers, a 530-metre main span and a 230-metre span on each side. It was built by Vinci Construction.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the Atlantic Bridge, where the phone icon marks the middle of the bridge outline, but only stop where it's legal and safe, because no pull-off is confirmed right there. Face back along the deck toward the Agua Clara side, then turn round for the Fort San Lorenzo side.

selfie_spots.name: Roadside clear space on the left after the Atlantic Bridge, toward Fort San Lorenzo
selfie_spots.detail: Cross the bridge, turn left immediately, and drive a few kilometres until you reach a clear space to park on your left
selfie_spots.why: It is the only spot a page names for stopping near the bridge, and that page says both sides of the bridge have good views.

sources.title: Atlantic Bridge - All You SHOULD Know Before Going (2026 Reviews), Tripadvisor

selfie_research.notes: I found no page that names a specific spot with the bridge directly behind a visitor, so the selfie spot above is the nearest supported option and is unverified for that purpose. The Tripadvisor text praises the views mainly for the canal locks, not for a bridge backdrop. Its parking clearing is described only by directions, not by a name. Evendo gives a walking route from central Colón to the bridge and says the bridge is a good photo backdrop at sunrise and sunset, but names no exact spot. A Viajenda page lists a 'Mirador de Isla Mamey' in a Colón album that also includes the bridge's inauguration, but no page I read says it frames the bridge, so I left it out. No page gave a 'ask someone' position, selfie stick or tripod rules, or a safety point. The coordinates you supplied (9.30790, -79.91798) are close to the bridge's listed position, which other pages put at roughly 9.307 N, 79.918 W.

card.hook: Everything at Agua Clara Locks is big: huge structures, long stretches of water and a whole lot of sky. A tiny human in the foreground is what makes people go "whoa" when they see your photo.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the Agua Clara Locks phone icon on the map, because it marks the spot itself and you're already in the right place. Face the water and the lock structures, and keep a railing, a sign or a friend near the bottom of your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit in the full width of the scene and all that sky. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the horizon up with one of the straight lines, because a tilted horizon is very obvious in a scene this straight and sharp.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh reflections on the water than midday. Check access details locally before you go.
card.selfie_here: Head to the raised end of the main viewing platform at the Agua Clara Locks Visitor Center, where the ground is higher and clear of the long metal fence. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the locks over your shoulder. The Agua Clara Sculpture sign by the canal walkway is another popular photo stop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand a little back from you while you stand at the raised end of the platform, so the lock chambers and control tower fit in behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is permitted throughout the visitor center and observation decks. Drones are strictly prohibited in the airspace around the Panama Canal expansion locks. Check for any access restrictions locally before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot with a friend tiny in the foreground, then a second with the same friend pretending to hold up the whole lock.
card.good_to_know: Agua Clara Locks are a lock complex on the Colón map. Weather can change quickly, so wipe your phone's camera glass before shooting, as damp air and drizzle can smear it. If something is moving through the scene, switch on Live Photos so you can pick the best moment afterwards.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the Agua Clara Locks phone icon on the map, because it marks the spot itself and you're already in the right place. Face the water and the lock structures, and keep a railing, a sign or a friend near the bottom of your frame.

selfie_research.notes: Sources are thin on exact selfie framing. No page states that the locks are behind the Agua Clara Sculpture sign, and the 'raised end' advice comes from a fence-and-view discussion, not a selfie guide. The ask-someone spot is my best reading of the platform descriptions, not a page's instruction. The aidventuro page says 'Panama City', but the landmark is in Colón province; its 'glass-walled observation deck' and 'mural near the entry' tips are unverified for this site. Reviews are dated (one from 2023, one 2,470 days old), and one page says the visitor center is under construction. No page mentions selfie sticks.

card.hook: Some buildings just line up for you, and this one has two matching bell towers that fit your phone screen like they were measured for it.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Avenida Amador Guerrero and Calle 5ta, with the cathedral just to the south. Face south toward the front of the building and let both towers fill the height of the screen.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the front. If the pavement is too narrow to step back, switch to 0.5x to fit both towers in, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the spires.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on your gridlines, line them up with the tower edges, and hold the phone level so the towers don't lean inwards.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the front. You'll often get fewer people on the street too.
card.selfie_here: We don't have a checked selfie spot here, so keep it simple. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x to fit more in, and put the building behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Colón has a reputation for high crime, and some sights are best photographed from a taxi rather than on foot, so keep your phone close and stay aware. It's an active church, so be respectful if a service is on, and check access before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get the doorway dead centre, both towers balanced, and a strip of street at the bottom of the frame?
card.good_to_know: This is the Catholic cathedral of Colón, a city in the north of Panama. It's the seat of the Diocese of Colón-Kuna Yala, created on 13 June 1997. The diocese belongs to the ecclesiastical province of Panama.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Avenida Amador Guerrero and Calle 5ta, with the cathedral just to the south. Face south toward the front of the building and let both towers fill the height of the screen.

selfie_research.safety: Wikivoyage describes Colón as notorious for its high crime rate, and advises that some sights are best photographed from a taxi rather than on foot.
selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a specific spot with the cathedral as the selfie backdrop, so I have not listed any selfie spot. Park-side lead, unverified: Harper's says the November 5 Park (known locally as 'La Concha') occupies a full block next to the cathedral, but no page calls it a photo spot. Ask-someone spot: Encircle Photos tags its front-view and profile-view cathedral photos at Avenida Amador Guerrero & Calle 5ta, but the page does not say where the photographer stood, so I left this null. Address discrepancy: most pages give Calle 5ta / Avenida Amador, but Wikivoyage places the cathedral 'round the corner at Calle 9' from Avenida Central/Calle 7. The Wikimedia Commons coordinates (9°21'39"N, 79°54'14"W) match the position you supplied. No page mentions selfie stick or tripod rules. card.hook: Some buildings don't need a clever trick. The Cristóbal Administration Building is one of them: step back, give it some sky, and let it do the posing.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 70 m north of the Cristóbal Administration Building, and face south. Keep the building in the middle of your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x and fit the whole width of the building in, with a bit of sky above and some ground below. If you can't step back far enough, try zoom 0.5x, but keep the building near the middle so the edges don't stretch. Then move closer and use zoom 2x or more for the entrance, windows or signs.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line them up with the edges of the building so the verticals stay nice and straight.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives you soft, flattering light. Skip the middle of the day if the sun is high and bright, because the sky can wash out.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, hold your phone a little higher than your face, and switch to zoom 0.5x if your phone offers it on the front. Turn so the building sits over your shoulder, and take a few shots to find your best one.
card.rules_and_safety: Check on arrival whether the area around the building is open to the public, and be considerate of others nearby. Access isn't stated for this spot, so it's worth checking locally.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot with straight lines, then one close-up of a detail, like a window or a sign, and see which one you like more.
card.good_to_know: In Spanish it's the Edificio de Administración de Cristóbal, and it's listed as a historic building. We don't have its history, size or dates here, so enjoy it as a simple, good-looking subject. It's about 1 minute on foot from where you turn to face south.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 70 m north of the Cristóbal Administration Building, and face south. Keep the building in the middle of your frame.

selfie_research.notes: No selfie spot, ask-someone spot, or photo-position guidance was found. The pages I found only identify the building: Mapcarta lists 'Edificio de Administración de Cristóbal' as a historic building near Parque 5 de noviembre and Plaza Cristobol (https://mapcarta.com/19769334). Wikimedia Commons has photos of it, with no advice on where to stand (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Edificio_de_Administraci%C3%B3n_de_Crist%C3%B3bal_(Puerto_de_Cristóbal).JPG). No travel blog, selfie guide, or tourism page named a spot, so I left the lists empty rather than guess. Rules on selfie sticks or tripods and safety were also not stated by any page found. Coordinates were not checked against a map.
